pedagogy.summary: Experimental vs theoretical bridges the two faces of probability: the theoretical value calculated from equally-likely outcomes, and the experimental value (relative frequency) measured from actual trials. The key idea is the law of large numbers in child form — as the number of trials grows, the experimental probability tends toward the theoretical, while short runs can differ wildly and each trial stays independent. The procedure is to run trials, compute relative frequencies from the data, and compare with prediction.
bestPractices: Have children compute relative frequency from THEIR OWN tally (frequency ÷ trials), not restate the theoretical value
Contrast a short run with a long run — pool class data or use a simulator — so convergence toward theory is seen, not asserted
Name explicitly that closeness improves with MORE trials but exact equality is not expected
Attack the 'due' fallacy directly: the die does not self-correct; relative frequency converges, absolute counts do not equalise exactly
Use the comparison to judge fairness sensibly — a big deviation over many trials suggests bias, a deviation over a few does not
keyRepresentations: Tally / frequency table with a relative-frequency column (f ÷ n)
Relative-frequency line converging toward the theoretical line as trials increase
Short-run vs long-run comparison side by side
Experimental value and theoretical value marked on the same 0-to-1 scale
commonMisconceptions: Expecting experimental results to equal the theoretical probability, and calling a device biased after a short run (law of small numbers)
Thinking absolute counts 'catch up' to become exactly equal with more trials (gambler's fallacy of convergence / the 'due' idea)
Reporting the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one (or vice versa)
Trusting a small sample as much as a large one to estimate an unknown probability

learn.summary: Learners compare experimental probability (relative frequency measured from actual trials) with theoretical probability (calculated from equally-likely outcomes). The central idea is a child-level law of large numbers: as the number of trials grows, the experimental relative frequency tends toward the theoretical value, while short runs can differ widely and each trial stays independent. Learners run trials, compute relative frequency from their OWN tally (frequency ÷ number of trials), and compare with prediction — and they confront two common fallacies: that experimental results should equal theory exactly, and that outcomes become 'due' or that absolute counts catch up to be equal.

activities.title: Roll, tally, and compute your own experimental probability
feedback: If a learner writes 1/6 for each outcome without using their tally, point out the task asked for the value from the rolls — re-establish: experimental = from your data (f ÷ n); theoretical = from the equally-likely outcomes.

If a learner calls the die loaded because a number came up 14 times instead of 10 in 60 rolls, acknowledge the deviation is real but note that a deviation of this size over only 60 trials is quite common for a fair die; deciding fairness needs many more trials.
If a learner expects the experimental values to match 1/6 exactly, affirm that close-not-exact is the normal and correct expectation for a fair die over a short run.
activities.rationale: Computing relative frequency from a learner's own data, rather than restating the theoretical value, is what makes the two meanings of probability distinct and exposes whether a learner confuses them. A short run of rolls is not enough to conclude bias, which is why the activity frames the deviation as expected.
sourceClaims: As the number of trials increases the relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability; a short run (e.g. 20 flips) is not enough to conclude a coin is biased, and combining more trials gives a more reliable estimate.
learnerActions: Roll a die 60 times (or flip a coin / spin a spinner), tallying each result in a frequency table.
Add a relative-frequency column: for each outcome compute frequency ÷ 60 as a fraction or decimal.
State the theoretical probability (1/6 for a fair die) and mark both the experimental and theoretical values on the same 0-to-1 scale.
Write in your own words how your experimental values compare with 1/6, and whether the differences you see are enough to call the die unfair.
activities.intendedInsight: Experimental probability comes from the data you collected (f ÷ n); it is usually close to but not exactly the theoretical value, and ordinary short-run differences are expected rather than proof of bias.

activities.title: Short run vs long run: watch the proportion settle while counts stay unequal
feedback: If a learner predicts exactly 100 of each number in 600 rolls, distinguish relative frequency (approaches 1/6) from raw counts (need not equalise); the proportions converge even though the counts stay unequal.

If a learner says a rarely-rolled number is 'due' to appear, state plainly that the die does not self-correct and each roll is independent — long-run convergence of proportions does not make any single outcome more likely on the next roll.

If a learner links convergence to sample size correctly, confirm that more trials give a more reliable estimate and that this is exactly how you would sensibly judge fairness: a big deviation over MANY trials suggests bias; a deviation over a few does not.
activities.rationale: Seeing a long run (pooled or simulated) lets convergence be observed rather than merely asserted, and displaying raw counts alongside proportions directly targets the gambler's-fallacy belief that counts equalise. Treating recency ('due') errors as a failure of independence is the documented misconception to confront.
sourceClaims: As the number of trials increases the relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability; a short run (e.g. 20 flips) is not enough to conclude a coin is biased, and combining more trials gives a more reliable estimate.

Recency errors (an outcome is 'due', or a streak will continue) reflect a failure to treat trials as independent, and belief in short-sequence representativeness makes people expect small samples to mirror the theoretical distribution.
learnerActions: Compare your own short run (60 rolls) with a much longer run — pool the whole class's tallies, or use a trials simulator set to 60, then 600, then 6000.
At each trial count, record both the relative frequency for each outcome AND the raw counts.
Predict before increasing the trials: 'If I roll 600 times instead of 60, will each number come up exactly 100 times?' Then check against the data.

Describe what gets closer to what: check whether, at the largest trial count, the relative frequencies for a fair die all sit near 1/6 (or near the theoretical value for your coin or spinner), while the raw counts (for example 995 vs 1020) are still unequal.
activities.intendedInsight: It is the PROPORTION (relative frequency) that converges toward the theoretical value with more trials — not the absolute counts becoming equal. No outcome is ever 'due', and each trial is independent of the ones before it.

activities.title: Judge a fairness claim from sample size
feedback: If a learner concludes bias from 14-out-of-60, redirect to the plan: extend the run or pool more trials, because bias needs many trials to judge and 14 against an expected 10 is within normal short-run variation.
If a learner trusts 20 flips as much as 500, point to the law-of-large-numbers idea: more trials give a more reliable estimate.
Confirm answers that propose collecting many more trials as the way to judge fairness much more reliably, and note that this gives strong evidence, not absolute certainty.
activities.rationale: Interpreting a fairness claim and ordering sample sizes tests the reasoning about MORE trials where the law-of-large-numbers understanding shows. This is interpretation work and does not itself generate the convergence experience, so it complements running trials rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: As the number of trials increases the relative frequency gets closer to the theoretical probability; a short run (e.g. 20 flips) is not enough to conclude a coin is biased, and combining more trials gives a more reliable estimate.

Recency errors (an outcome is 'due', or a streak will continue) reflect a failure to treat trials as independent, and belief in short-sequence representativeness makes people expect small samples to mirror the theoretical distribution.
learnerActions: Read a scenario: 'A 4 came up 14 times in 60 rolls of a die.' Decide whether this proves the die is biased, and explain your reasoning.
Decide whose data you would trust more to estimate the chance of an outcome for a possibly-bent coin: 20 flips or 500 flips, and say why.
Order several sample sizes from least to most reliable for estimating an unknown probability.
Explain how you WOULD decide, with much more confidence, whether the die is loaded — and why even many trials give strong evidence rather than absolute certainty.
activities.intendedInsight: A small sample is not as trustworthy as a large one for estimating an unknown probability; a single ordinary deviation over few trials is not evidence of bias, and judging fairness sensibly depends on the number of trials behind the data.

constraints: Learners must compute relative frequency from their OWN tally (frequency ÷ trials), not restate the theoretical value.
Name explicitly that closeness to theory improves with MORE trials but exact equality is not expected — and that it is the proportion that converges, not the counts that equalise.
Confront the 'due' fallacy directly: the die does not self-correct and each trial is independent; relative frequency converges while absolute counts do not equalise exactly.

A multiple-choice or ordering item can assess reading a convergence graph or judging a fairness claim from sample size, but it cannot let a learner run and scale trials — so recognition items should supplement, not replace, actually running experiments.

An interpretation-only or discussion-only activity can analyse convergence but does not itself generate the long-run experience; learners still need to run or pool trials to see the proportion settle.

Optional interactive scaffold: a die/coin/spinner simulator with a slider or buttons for 20, 60, 600, 6000 trials, plotting a live experimental relative-frequency line against the theoretical line plus a raw-count display, makes the convergence mechanism concrete. This is one helpful way to show the effect, not a required mechanism — pooling class tallies serves the same purpose.
Use fairness judgement sensibly: a big deviation over many trials suggests bias; a deviation over a few does not.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source framed a 3D dice-roller as adding 'little' and static images / dialogue as 'poor' because they cannot run trials. The genuine objective limit retained here is only that recognition-only or non-running formats do not themselves generate the long-run convergence experience; claims that extra dimensions 'buy little' or that a static image 'cannot teach this' were catalog preferences and have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements, not universal laws.

Self-audit of arithmetic and probability logic: for 60 rolls of a fair die the expected count per outcome is 10 (60 × 1/6); experimental relative frequencies are each frequency ÷ 60; theoretical is 1/6 ≈ 0.167. For 600 rolls the expected count is 100 each, but exactly 100 each is NOT expected — only that relative frequencies approach 1/6. These are consistent across the source and reproduced faithfully. The example raw counts (e.g. 995 vs 1020, 980 vs 1015) are illustrative of 'unequal counts at large n' and are plausible for large die runs; they are kept as illustrations, not as guaranteed results.

Independent editor re-audit: no critical learner-facing factual or logic errors were found. The convergence-of-proportions-vs-counts distinction, the independence/'due' framing, and the sample-size reasoning are internally coherent across summary, actions, insights and feedback; the '14 vs expected 10 in 60 rolls' is correctly treated as within normal short-run variation.

probeDeeper: Your 4 came up 14 times, not 10 — does that prove the die is loaded? How could you decide for sure?
If you rolled 600 times, would each number come up exactly 100 times? What exactly gets closer to what?
What's the difference between the probability you calculated from your rolls and the 1/6 you expected?
Whose data would you trust more to estimate a bent coin's chance — 20 flips or 500 flips? Why?
assess.correctAnswer: A correct performance: computes each experimental probability as that number's frequency ÷ 60 from the actual tally, notes the values are close to but not exactly 1/6, explains the differences as normal short-run variation, and predicts that 600 rolls would bring the relative frequencies CLOSER to 1/6 — not that each number lands exactly 100 times.

errorPatterns.pattern: Expects experimental results to equal the theoretical value and concludes bias from a short run
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach the mechanics — extend the run (or pool data) so the relative frequency settles nearer 1/6; a deviation over few trials is expected, bias needs many trials to judge
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the die loaded because a number came up 14 rather than 10 times in 60 rolls

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks absolute counts 'catch up' to become exactly equal with more trials (the 'due' / gambler's fallacy of convergence)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish relative frequency (approaches 1/6) from raw counts (need NOT equalise); show a long simulation where proportions converge but counts stay unequal, and each roll remains independent
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts exactly 100 of each number in 600 rolls, or says a rarely-rolled number is 'due' to appear

errorPatterns.pattern: Reports the theoretical probability when asked for the experimental one (or vice versa)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-establish the two meanings: experimental = from the data you collected (f ÷ n); theoretical = from the equally-likely outcomes; the task asked for the one from the rolls
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked for the experimental probability from their tally, answers 1/6 instead of computing frequency ÷ 60

responseLevels.gap: States the theoretical 1/6 regardless of the data, or expects an exact match; treats any deviation as proof of bias; no relative-frequency computed from the tally
responseLevels.full: Computes relative frequency from the data, treats deviations as short-run variation, and predicts that more trials bring the relative frequency CLOSER to theoretical without the counts becoming exactly equal or any outcome being 'due'
responseLevels.partial: Computes experimental probabilities and knows they differ from theoretical, but expects exact convergence (100 each at 600) or reads ordinary variation as bias — describes results without correctly linking convergence to sample size

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a die and have them roll it 60 times, tallying each result. Then say: 'Work out the experimental probability of each number from your results. How do they compare with what you'd expect for a fair die? And what would you expect if you rolled 600 times instead of 60?' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they compute relative frequency from THEIR data or just state 1/6, whether they treat a deviation as proof of bias, and whether they think 600 rolls would give exactly 100 each.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching separates the child who computes relative frequency from their own data and expects closer-not-exact convergence from one who just recites 1/6, calls the die biased on an ordinary deviation, or expects exactly 100 of each at 600 rolls. The reasoning about MORE trials is where the law-of-large-numbers understanding shows.

Recency errors (an outcome is 'due', or a streak will continue) reflect a failure to treat trials as independent, and belief in short-sequence representativeness makes people expect small samples to mirror the theoretical distribution.
